title: Come and see
hook: many practice without taking refuge; the teaching invites you to come and see
carry: the lamp shows, the seeing is yours

segments.voice: Yesterday: yana, the Buddhists you'll meet, and your line, many doors. Did you get to ask someone what their practice looks like? Day three hundred twenty-five.

There's a certain kind of cook who, when you ask what's in the soup, doesn't explain. She just hands you a spoon. Don't take my word for it. Taste. It's a confident thing to do: it only works if the soup is good. This week has been about practicing with people, finding a sangha, a friend, a temple, maybe taking refuge someday. But plenty of people practice for years without any of that, and the teaching doesn't check anyone's ID at the door. It hands you a spoon. Today: come and see.
screen: `WHAT'S IN THE SOUP?` → `SHE HANDS YOU A SPOON.` → `TASTE IT YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: In Theravada temples and homes, people chant a short list of the qualities of the Buddha's teaching. In Pali it begins: "Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, sandiṭṭhiko, akāliko, ehipassiko." In plain English: the teaching is well spoken by the Blessed One, visible here and now, not a matter of time, and ehipassiko. Ehi means come. Passa means see. Ehipassiko is a word made from an invitation: the teaching is the come-and-see kind. Not come and believe. Not come and sign. Come and see. The same list goes on to say it leads onward, and that the wise know it for themselves. You heard the same spirit with the Kalamas: test it yourself. And in the old discourses, a listener often ends by saying something like, it's as if you set upright what was overturned, or held up a lamp in the dark so those with eyes could see. The lamp shows. The seeing is yours. That's one reason people can practice without any label. Some take refuge and some never do. Some come to the teaching through a temple and some through a library book or an app like this one. The invitation doesn't change. That closes this stretch of the path, about practicing alongside other people, and it closes on an open door. Tomorrow we begin the big lookout: six days to look back at the whole year, starting with the stories.
screen: `THE QUALITIES OF THE TEACHING.` · `EHI, COME. PASSA, SEE.` · `A LAMP HELD UP IN THE DARK.` · `NO LABEL NEEDED.` · then, large: `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, practice with no labels at all. You're not a Buddhist or a non-Buddhist for the next two minutes. You're just someone breathing, seeing what's here. Watch one breath all the way in and all the way out. Does watching it bring a little more ease, or not? Don't decide in advance. Come and see. The bell holds the time.
Ehipassiko. Come and see: the teaching invites you to look for yourself, not to believe first.
Your line: the lamp shows, the seeing is yours. Today, practice one thing from this year without calling it anything, and watch what it does. Day three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the qualities of the Dhamma, including ehipassiko, in their devotions; teachers across traditions welcome people to practice without taking refuge or calling themselves Buddhist.

fork.setup: a friend is curious about meditation but says, I'm not Buddhist and don't want to be. what does ehipassiko suggest you say?
options: you don't need a label; try it and see what it does.
fork.reveal: the teaching calls itself the come-and-see kind: it invites looking, not signing up.

original.note: Pali ehipassiko: from ehi (come) + passa (see): the come-and-see kind.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slogan for skeptics.
what it means: one of the teaching's own qualities, chanted in devotions: it invites you to look for yourself.
what a scholar hears: ehipassiko turns the imperative 'ehi passa', 'come, see!', into an adjective; it stands in the Dhamma recollection (dhammānussati) between akāliko and opanayiko.
